questions.problem:
A seller delivers bricks on pallets. One pallet contains $500$ bricks. The weight of a brick is normally distributed with a mean of $3\,\text{lb}$ and a standard deviation of $0.25\,\text{lb},$ while the weight of a pallet is normally distributed with a mean of $40\,\text{lb}$ and a standard deviation of $4\,\text{lb}.$ If one pallet with bricks is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs less than $1\,545\,\text{lb}?$ You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7324\,$ | $\,0.7357\,$ | $\,0.7389\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ | $\,0.7704\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ | $\,0.7995\,$ | $\,0.8023\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th brick, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a pallet. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(3,{0.25}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 500,
$$

and

$$
Y∼N(40,{4}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected pallet with bricks. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{500}+Y,
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =500\cdot 3+40 \\  & =1\,540, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =500\cdot {0.25}^{2}+{4}^{2} \\  & =47.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(1\,540,47.25).
$$

In order to find $P(W<1\,545),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<1\,545) & =P(Z<\frac{1\,545-1\,540}{\sqrt{47.25}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<0.73) \\  & =Φ(0.73)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.73)≈0.7673.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<1\,545) & ≈Φ(0.73) \\  & ≈0.7673.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{20}$ are I.I.D random variables, where

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(1,{2}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 20,
$$

what is the distribution of $Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{20}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{20}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{20}$ are mutually independent, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{20} & ∼N(20\cdot 1,\,20\cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(20\cdot 1,\,20\cdot 4) \\  & =N(20,80).\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{20}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{20}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{20} & ∼N(20\cdot 1,\,20\cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(20\cdot 1,\,20\cdot 4) \\  & =N(20,80).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(Y\le 21).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le 21) & =P(Z\le \frac{21-20}{\sqrt{80}}) \\  & =P(Z\le \frac{1}{\sqrt{80}}) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.11) \\  & =Φ(0.11)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(0.11)=0.5438.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Y\le 21)=Φ(0.11)=0.5438.
$$

questions.problem:
In a particular shop, cables are sold in coils. The length of the cable in a coil is normally distributed with a mean of $50\,\text{m}$ and a standard deviation of $0.7\,\text{m}.$ If John bought $5$ coils, what is the probability that the total length of the cables he bought is greater than $250\,\text{m}$ and less than $253\,m?$ You may assume that the lengths of the cable in the coils are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.7\,$ | $\,0.9554\,$ | $\,0.9564\,$ | $\,0.9573\,$ | $\,0.9582\,$ |
| $\,1.8\,$ | $\,0.9641\,$ | $\,0.9649\,$ | $\,0.9656\,$ | $\,0.9664\,$ |
| $\,1.9\,$ | $\,0.9713\,$ | $\,0.9719\,$ | $\,0.9726\,$ | $\,0.9732\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the length of cable in the $i$th coil. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(50,{0.7}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 5.
$$

Let the random variable $L$ denote the total length of the cables in $5$ randomly selected coils. Then, since

$$
L={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{5},
$$

we have that $L$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[L] & =5\cdot 50 \\  & =250, \\ \text{Var}[L] & =5\cdot {0.7}^{2} \\  & =2.45.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
L∼N(250,2.45).
$$

In order to find $P(250<L<253),$ we convert $L$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(250<L<253) & =P(\frac{250-250}{\sqrt{2.45}}<Z<\frac{253-250}{\sqrt{2.45}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<1.92) \\  & =Φ(1.92)-Φ(0) \\  & =Φ(1.92)-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.92)≈0.9726.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(250<L<253) & ≈Φ(0.95)-0.5 \\  & ≈0.4726.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Fred picked $10$ watermelons from his vegetable garden. The weight of watermelons he grows is normally distributed with a mean of $11\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $3\,\text{kg}.$ What is the probability that the total weight of the watermelons Fred picked is greater than $100\,\text{kg}$ and less than $110\,\text{kg}?$ You may assume that the weights of the watermelons are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8461\,$ | $\,0.8485\,$ | $\,0.8508\,$ | $\,0.8531\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8686\,$ | $\,0.8708\,$ | $\,0.8729\,$ | $\,0.8749\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8888\,$ | $\,0.8907\,$ | $\,0.8925\,$ | $\,0.8944\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th watermelon. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(11,{3}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 10.
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denotes the total weight of the $10$ watermelons. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{10},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =10\cdot 11 \\  & =110, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =10\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(110,90).
$$

In order to find $P(100<W<110),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<W<110) & =P(\frac{100-110}{\sqrt{90}}<Z<\frac{110-110}{\sqrt{90}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.05<Z<0) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-1.05) \\  & =Φ(0)-(1-Φ(1.05)) \\  & =0.5-(1-Φ(1.05)) \\  & =Φ(1.05)-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.05)≈0.8531.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<W<110) & ≈Φ(1.05)-0.5 \\  & ≈0.3531.\end{aligned}
$$
